title: Bayesian Inference
intro: Bayesian inference treats an unknown parameter as a random variable. A prior distribution expresses what is believed before the data; Bayes' theorem combines it with the likelihood into a posterior, from which every conclusion follows.

blocks.text: This is Bayes' Theorem (#/probability/foundations/bayes-theorem) with a continuum of hypotheses. The denominator, the marginal likelihood, is often intractable; the proportionality is enough to find the shape of the posterior, and Markov chain Monte Carlo can sample from it without the constant (Monte Carlo Methods (#/probability/limit-theorems/monte-carlo)).

items: Beta prior with binomial data: a Beta($a, b$) prior and $k$ successes in $n$ trials give a Beta($a + k$, $b + n - k$) posterior. The prior acts like $a$ earlier successes and $b$ earlier failures.
Gamma prior with Poisson data: Gamma($a, b$) and counts summing to $S$ over $n$ periods give Gamma($a + S$, $b + n$).
Normal prior with normal data of known variance: the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data, and precisions (inverse variances) add.

blocks.text: Conjugacy makes the update a matter of adding counts, and shows the key behaviours plainly: with little data the prior matters; with much data the likelihood dominates and different reasonable priors lead to the same posterior; the posterior spread shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$.

A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with posterior probability 0.95, a direct statement about the parameter that a confidence interval does not make. The posterior predictive distribution averages the model over the posterior; for a beta–binomial model the probability that the next trial succeeds is the posterior mean $(a + k)/(a + b + n)$, which with a uniform prior is Laplace's rule of succession $(k + 1)/(n + 2)$.

widget.title: Updating a belief about a coin

blocks.text: Try it: with the defaults, a Beta(2, 2) prior and 7 heads in 10 flips give a Beta(9, 5) posterior centred near 0.64. Make the prior strong (a = b = 20) and the same data barely move it. Then scale the data to 140 heads in 200 and the posterior is narrow and centred on 0.7 whatever the prior: data overwhelm the prior.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
# Beta-binomial: prior Beta(2, 2) on a coin's heads probability, then 7 heads in 10 flips
a, b, k, n = 2, 2, 7, 10
post = stats.beta(a + k, b + n - k)
print(f"posterior Beta({a + k}, {b + n - k}): mean {post.mean():.4f}, mode {(a + k - 1) / (a + b + n - 2):.4f}, MLE {k/n}")
lo, hi = post.ppf([0.025, 0.975])
print(f"95% credible interval ({lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}); P(p > 0.5 | data) = {post.sf(0.5):.4f}")
# Posterior predictive probability that the next flip is heads = posterior mean
print(f"P(next flip heads | data) = {(a + k) / (a + b + n):.4f}")
# Sequential updating gives the same answer as one batch update
rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
flips = rng.random(200) < 0.7
aa, bb = a, b
for f in flips: aa, bb = aa + f, bb + (1 - f)
print(f"after 200 flips one at a time: Beta({aa}, {bb}); in one batch: Beta({a + flips.sum()}, {b + 200 - flips.sum()})")
print(f"posterior sd shrinks like 1/sqrt(n): {stats.beta(aa, bb).std():.4f}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: with prior Beta(2, 2) and 7 heads in 10, the posterior is Beta(9, 5), with mean 0.643, mode 0.667 (the MLE is 0.7), a 95% credible interval (0.386, 0.861) and $P(p > 0.5\mid\text{data}) = 0.867$. Updating one flip at a time over 200 flips gives the same Beta(142, 62) as one batch update, with posterior standard deviation 0.032.

blocks.title: Three for three
blocks.text: With a uniform prior on a coin's heads probability, you see 3 heads in 3 flips. Find the posterior and the probability that the next flip is heads.
solution: Predictive probability = posterior mean $4/5 = 0.8$ (Laplace's rule $(3 + 1)/(3 + 2)$). The MLE would say 1, which is overconfident.

blocks.title: Normal–normal updating
blocks.text: Prior $\theta\sim N(0, 1)$; one observation $x\sim N(\theta, 1)$. Find the posterior.
solution: Precisions add: $1 + 1 = 2$, so the posterior variance is $1/2$.
The posterior mean is the precision-weighted average: $(1\cdot0 + 1\cdot x)/2 = x/2$. Posterior $N(x/2, 1/2)$.

blocks.title: Credible versus confidence
blocks.text: A 95% confidence interval for $p$ is (0.41, 0.59). Can you say $P(0.41 < p < 0.59) = 0.95$?
solution: Not in the frequentist framework: $p$ is fixed, and 95% describes how often the procedure's intervals cover it.
A Bayesian 95% credible interval does support that statement, given the prior. For large samples with weak priors the two intervals nearly coincide numerically.
